articles.title: RSV vaccines slash infections: data show jabs’ staggering success against dangerous virus
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03573-3Vaccines and monoclonal-antibody injections are cutting hospitalizations linked to the respiratory virus.
articles.content:
Protection against the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) must expand to lower-income countries, which are harder hit.Credit: Hailshadow/Getty

“Something’s wrong with the data. There are too few people in hospitals” with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), epidemiologist Caroline Klint Johannesen recalls a colleague remarking while analysing Danish health records for last winter.

On 1 October 2025, Denmark introduced a nationwide policy of vaccinating pregnant people against RSV — a respiratory pathogen that usually causes mild symptoms but can lead to severe disease and even death in vulnerable people, including infants and older adults. Maternal antibodies induced by the vaccine cross the placenta to protect babies for around the first six months of their lives, when they are most at risk. Newborns at high risk of severe disease, including premature infants, whose mothers had not been vaccinated, were given injections of monoclonal antibodies.

RSV wave hammers hospitals — but vaccines and treatments are coming

Johannesen, a vaccine researcher at Nordsjællands Hospital in Hillerød, Denmark, found1 that infant hospital admissions plummeted. The immunizations are working, she says (see ‘Newborn protection’).

Global risks

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that every year, RSV hospitalizes roughly 3.6 million and kills about 100,000 children under 5 years old. Of these deaths, 97% occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).

The virus is also dangerous to older adults — although those risks are widely underappreciated by both physicians and the public. Historically, testing has been sparse, and there are no global statistics for RSV-related adult deaths. But over the age of 60, hospitalizations and mortality increase with age, especially in people with other diseases such as chronic heart and lung conditions. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that between around 10,000 and 25,000 people have died in each of the past two winters, especially in older age groups.

Source: Ref. 1

Since 2022, when European regulators approved nirsevimab — a long-acting monoclonal antibody against RSV — a second antibody and three vaccines have been developed for use in adults, one of which is suitable for pregnant people.

“It’s just remarkable,” says Buddy Creech, a paediatrician at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee, to have gone “from no mechanism to prevent RSV to an embarrassment of riches”. Dozens of countries across Europe, Asia and North and South America have launched various immunization programmes.

Up-to-date immunizations
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant real-world impact of RSV vaccines and monoclonal antibodies in drastically reducing hospitalizations and deaths, especially among vulnerable infants and older adults. The introduction of maternal vaccination policies and new treatments represents a major breakthrough in preventing a dangerous respiratory virus with global significance. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights broad public health benefits and ongoing global efforts to expand protection.

The vaccine helps mothers pass protective antibodies to their babies, shielding them during their first six months. Babies at high risk who did not get this protection received special antibody injections. Researchers found that hospital admissions for infants dropped sharply after these measures were introduced.

**Impact** – This is one of the first clear examples showing that RSV vaccines and antibody treatments work well in the real world. It means fewer babies have to go to the hospital, and fewer people suffer severe illness. The success in Denmark encourages other countries to start similar programs. Older adults, another group at risk, now have new vaccines and treatments available too.

**What's next step** – Efforts are growing to bring these vaccines and treatments to more countries, especially lower-income ones where RSV causes the most deaths. Scientists and health groups are working to make sure more people, including older adults, get protected through vaccination programs.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Vaccinating pregnant people and using new antibody treatments have significantly lowered RSV hospital visits, showing a powerful way to protect babies and vulnerable adults from this serious virus.

articles.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
articles.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.
articles.content:
When muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue. But scientists have discovered that without one critical protein, this repair system can break down, leaving injured muscles filled with fat and scar tissue instead of healthy muscle.

Researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes. Their findings suggest that TRF2 is also essential for maintaining the identity of muscle stem cells, allowing them to continue repairing and regenerating muscle throughout life.

The discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide new directions for muscular dystrophy treatments. It may also help scientists understand important differences between muscle regeneration and cancer, including why skeletal muscle can repair itself so effectively while cancers originating in muscle are relatively uncommon.

"For years, TRF2 has been viewed as a protein whose primary job is protecting the ends of chromosomes from damage or corruption," said senior author Foteini Mourkioti, PhD, an associate professor of Orthopedic Surgery at Penn Medicine. "But rather than simply protecting DNA, TRF2 seems to be key to regenerating muscle throughout life."

A Hidden Protein With an Unexpected Role in Muscle Repair

For years, scientists have studied TRF2 because of its role in safeguarding telomeres, the protective structures found at the ends of chromosomes. Chromosomes carry our genetic information, and telomeres help keep their ends from deteriorating or being mistaken for damaged DNA.

The new research shows that TRF2 has another important responsibility. It helps muscle stem cells retain the genetic instructions that make them muscle stem cells in the first place. Maintaining that identity is essential because these specialized cells serve as the body's reserve supply for repairing injured muscle.

Under normal conditions, muscle stem cells spend much of their time inactive. When an injury occurs, they become active, multiply, and help replace damaged muscle tissue. Some then return to a resting state, preserving a population of stem cells that can respond to future injuries.

Through laboratory experiments, the researchers found that TRF2 levels change as muscle stem cells move between these different stages. The protein's activity rises and falls as the cells transition from dormancy to repair and then replenish themselves, suggesting that TRF2 helps regulate the entire regeneration process.

Without TRF2, Damaged Muscles Accumulate Fat and Scar Tissue

To understand how important TRF2 is, the scientists removed the protein from muscle stem cells in laboratory mice. At first, the animals' muscles appeared normal, suggesting that the loss of TRF2 did not immediately damage existing muscle tissue.

Over time, however, a serious problem emerged. The population of functional muscle stem cells began to decline, leaving the animals increasingly unable to repair damaged muscle.

The researchers initially expected the cells to die, since losing TRF2 can produce that outcome in other tissues. Instead, they discovered something more surprising: the cells remained alive but lost the molecular identity that allowed them to function as muscle stem cells.

In effect, the cells no longer maintained the biological program needed to perform their specialized repair duties.

The consequences became clear when the muscles were injured. Rather than rebuilding healthy muscle, the damaged tissue accumulated fat and scar tissue, a form of tissue replacement that cannot restore normal muscle function.

"This completely changes how we think about TRF2's role in these cells," said Mourkioti. "The loss of identity has severe implications for whether recovery from injury is even possible."

A Potential Breakthrough for Muscular Dystrophy Research

The team also investigated whether TRF2 plays a role in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a serious inherited disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. The disease interferes with the body's ability to maintain healthy muscles, making effective repair especially important.

Using a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the researchers removed TRF2 from muscle stem cells and observed a dramatic worsening of the disease.

Muscle degeneration progressed much faster, and the affected mice had shorter survival times. These findings indicate that TRF2 plays an important role in preserving the regenerative capacity of muscles already struggling with a serious genetic disease.

The results do not yet establish a new treatment for muscular dystrophy. However, they identify a biological mechanism that researchers may eventually be able to target to help preserve muscle stem cell function and improve tissue repair.

How TRF2 Protects the Identity of Muscle Stem Cells

Further experiments revealed how TRF2 performs this unexpected function.

Although the protein is best known for working at the ends of chromosomes, the researchers found that it also attaches to regulatory regions throughout the genome. These regions help control which genes are active or inactive, determining how cells behave and what specialized functions they perform.

For muscle stem cells, this regulation is particularly important. Their ability to repair muscle depends on maintaining a specific pattern of gene activity that preserves their identity and regenerative potential.

The scientists discovered that many of the DNA regions associated with TRF2 contain unusual structures known as G-quadruplexes. These structures form when sections of DNA rich in the building block guanine fold into distinctive arrangements involving four interacting strands or segments.

G-quadruplexes have attracted considerable scientific interest because they can influence how genes function. They are also being investigated as possible targets for cancer treatments.

The Penn researchers found that TRF2 interacts with these specialized DNA structures to help maintain the genetic program that keeps muscle stem cells functioning properly.

"We found that TRF2 works through these secondary DNA structures to preserve the identity of muscle stem cells and keep them capable of repairing damaged muscle," Mourkioti said. "That was completely unexpected."

What Muscle Regeneration Could Reveal About Cancer

Beyond muscular dystrophy, the discovery may help researchers investigate a longstanding mystery about muscle biology.

Skeletal muscle, the type of muscle that allows the body to move, has an impressive ability to regenerate after injury. Yet cancers that originate in skeletal muscle are relatively rare, even though other tissues with substantial regenerative activity can be more vulnerable to cancer.

This raises an important question: how can muscle maintain such a powerful repair system without frequently developing cancer?

The researchers believe that TRF2's unusual role in muscle stem cells could offer clues. By examining how the protein regulates gene activity in muscle compared with other tissues, scientists may gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that support regeneration while limiting the risk of uncontrolled cell growth.

That distinction matters because cancer develops when cells acquire changes that allow them to grow and divide without the normal biological restraints. Finding ways to strengthen muscle repair without encouraging abnormal growth would be an important goal for future therapies.

Mourkioti and her colleagues are now investigating whether the way muscle stem cells use TRF2 could lead to new treatment strategies for muscular dystrophy. They also hope to determine what this mechanism can reveal about cancer biology in tissues that are more susceptible to the disease.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these findings can be translated into treatments for people, the discovery reveals an important part of the body's muscle repair system. It also demonstrates that a protein long associated with protecting DNA has a much broader role in keeping muscles capable of healing.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health/ National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (R01 DK123356, R01s CA174904, GM101149, and FDN-143330).

articles.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
articles.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
articles.content:
Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."

The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

articles.personality_title_fr: L'IA améliore la technologie des yeux bioniques pour restaurer la vue des aveugles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Des scientifiques travaillent à restaurer la vue des personnes aveugles. Une méthode utilise des implants qui envoient des signaux électriques directement au cortex visuel, la partie du cerveau qui traite la vision. Cela aide les personnes dont les yeux ou les nerfs optiques sont endommagés mais dont le cerveau peut encore répondre.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'Université de Californie à Santa Barbara et d'autres universités ont utilisé l'intelligence artificielle (IA) pour améliorer le fonctionnement d'un implant cérébral chez un homme aveugle de 27 ans en Espagne. Il avait 96 petits électrodes implantées dans son cortex visuel. L'IA a appris comment son cerveau réagissait aux signaux électriques et a aidé à créer des motifs produisant des formes et des éclairs de lumière plus clairs, appelés phosphènes, qu'il pouvait voir.

**Impact** – C’est important car cela montre que l’IA peut rendre la technologie des yeux bioniques plus précise et personnalisée. Au lieu d’utiliser des réglages fixes, l’implant peut s’adapter à la façon dont le cerveau de chaque personne réagit. Cela pourrait aider à créer de meilleurs dispositifs qui donnent aux aveugles des expériences visuelles plus constantes et significatives.

**Prochaines étapes** – L’équipe de recherche prévoit de continuer à tester et améliorer ce système d’IA chez plus de personnes. Ils espèrent que les futurs dispositifs pourront non seulement envoyer des signaux mais aussi lire les réponses du cerveau et s’ajuster automatiquement. Cela pourrait conduire à une meilleure restauration de la vue pour les personnes ayant perdu la vue à cause d’une blessure ou d’une maladie.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Utiliser l’IA pour adapter les implants cérébraux aux réponses individuelles du cerveau rapproche de la possibilité d’aider les aveugles à voir de nouveau grâce aux yeux bioniques.
articles.personality_title_es: La IA mejora la tecnología de ojos biónicos para restaurar la vista a personas ciegas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estado trabajando para devolver la vista a personas ciegas. Un método usa implantes que envían señales eléctricas directamente a la corteza visual del cerebro, la parte que procesa lo que vemos. Esto ayuda a personas cuyos ojos o nervios ópticos están dañados, pero cuyo cerebro aún puede responder.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de California en Santa Bárbara y otras instituciones usaron inteligencia artificial (IA) para mejorar cómo funciona un implante cerebral en un hombre ciego de 27 años en España. Tenía 96 electrodos pequeños implantados en su corteza visual. La IA aprendió cómo respondía su cerebro a las señales eléctricas y ayudó a crear patrones que producían luces y formas más claras, llamadas fosfenos, que él podía ver.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque muestra que la IA puede hacer la tecnología de ojos biónicos más precisa y personalizada. En lugar de usar configuraciones fijas, el implante puede adaptarse a cómo reacciona el cerebro de cada persona. Esto podría ayudar a crear dispositivos mejores que den a las personas ciegas experiencias visuales más constantes y útiles.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo de investigación planea seguir probando y mejorando este sistema de IA en más personas. Esperan que los futuros dispositivos no solo envíen señales, sino que también lean las respuestas del cerebro y se ajusten automáticamente. Esto podría llevar a una mejor restauración de la vista para personas que la perdieron por lesiones o enfermedades.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Usar IA para adaptar implantes cerebrales a las respuestas individuales del cerebro acerca la posibilidad de ayudar a personas ciegas a ver de nuevo con ojos biónicos.

articles.title: Novel CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03705-9Earlier CRISPR treatments require removal of a participant’s cells, a complex and costly approach.
articles.content:
The Cas9 protein together with RNA and DNA (orange; artist’s illustration). A new therapy uses the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system to treat a rare genetic disease called hereditary angioedema.Credit: Alfred Pasieka/Science Photo Library

A pioneering therapy that edits genes inside a recipient’s body continues to be effective four years after treatment, according to data released by its developer, Intellia Therapeutics.

The therapy, named lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z), was designed to treat one form of a genetic disorder that causes episodes of painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and other parts of the body. Lonvo-z deploys the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing system to disable the gene that produces prekallikrein, a protein made in the liver that promotes blood-vessel leakage.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Intellia, headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has applied for approval of lonvo-z to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is expected to issue a decision by 10 March. If approved, the therapy will become the world’s first CRISPR medicine to be delivered directly inside the body, or in vivo, John Leonard, Intellia’s chief executive, told investors on 12 November. Currently, the only CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA is performed on cells that have first been removed from the body and are subsequently re-infused.

For people with the condition, hereditary angioedema, the gene-editing approach could offer relief from a lifetime of juggling medications to prevent and treat swelling attacks, says Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial. “It’s very reassuring,” he says of the four-year data. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.”

Inside job

The only approved CRISPR therapy is Casgevy, a treatment for two genetic blood disorders, sickle cell anemia and ß-thalassemia. To create a dose of Casgevy, physicians first remove blood stem cells from the recipient, then send them off for gene editing. The edited cells are infused back into the recipient.

The therapy must be made anew for each person, adding time, cost, and complexity. The recipient also has to undergo harsh chemotherapy treatment to make room for the edited cells.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

In vivo gene-editing approaches aim to sidestep these concerns by editing genes directly in the body. Lonvo-z, for example, consists of fatty particles that encase mRNA encoding CRISPR-Cas9 components. The particles are infused into the blood and taken up by the liver, where prekallikrein is produced. The procedure takes one day.

In vivo gene editing can introduce other safety concerns, however. The therapy affords no opportunity to screen out cells with unwanted edits at other locations in the genome, or in other organs. Recipients might also have harmful immune responses to the treatment.

Last year, the FDA placed a clinical hold on two other in vivo studies sponsored by Intellia after a participant — an older man with other health conditions — developed liver damage and died after receiving a CRISPR treatment. The FDA lifted the hold this year after requiring added safety measures.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a pioneering in vivo CRISPR gene-editing therapy that has shown sustained effectiveness over four years and is poised to become the first FDA-approved treatment of its kind. This represents a major breakthrough in genetic medicine with broad potential to improve the lives of patients with hereditary angioedema and possibly other genetic diseases. The therapy offers a simpler, less costly alternative to existing ex vivo CRISPR treatments, with significant implications for patient care and gene therapy advancement.
articles.personality_title: First in-body CRISPR gene therapy nears FDA approval after 4 years of success
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Hereditary angioedema is a rare genetic disease causing painful swelling in the throat and other body parts. Current gene therapies using CRISPR technology must remove and edit cells outside the body before returning them, making treatment complex and costly.

**What happened** – Intellia Therapeutics developed a new treatment called lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z) that edits genes directly inside the body. This therapy uses tiny fat particles to deliver the CRISPR system to the liver, turning off a gene that causes swelling. Data shows the treatment remains effective four years after a single infusion. Intellia has applied to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for approval, with a decision expected by March 10, 2027.

**Impact** – If approved, lonvo-z will be the first CRISPR therapy delivered inside the body, simplifying treatment and reducing costs compared to current methods. Patients with hereditary angioedema could avoid lifelong medication and complicated procedures. This approach might also open the door to easier gene therapies for other diseases.

**What's next step** – The FDA will review the safety and effectiveness data before deciding on approval. Meanwhile, researchers will continue monitoring patients and working on improving in-body gene editing to minimize risks like unintended genetic changes or immune reactions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new gene therapy that edits genes directly inside the body shows lasting success and could soon become the first FDA-approved in vivo CRISPR treatment for hereditary angioedema.
articles.personality_title_fr: Première thérapie génique CRISPR directe en cours d'approbation par la FDA après 4 ans de succès
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’angio-œdème héréditaire est une maladie génétique rare provoquant des gonflements douloureux dans la gorge et d’autres parties du corps. Les thérapies géniques actuelles utilisant CRISPR doivent retirer et modifier les cellules à l’extérieur du corps avant de les réinjecter, ce qui rend le traitement complexe et coûteux.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Intellia Therapeutics a développé un nouveau traitement appelé lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z) qui modifie les gènes directement à l’intérieur du corps. Cette thérapie utilise de petites particules grasses pour transporter le système CRISPR vers le foie afin d’arrêter un gène responsable du gonflement. Les données montrent que le traitement reste efficace quatre ans après une seule injection. Intellia a demandé l’approbation de la Food and Drug Administration (FDA) des États-Unis, avec une décision attendue pour le 10 mars 2027.

**Impact** – Si elle est approuvée, lonvo-z sera la première thérapie CRISPR administrée directement dans le corps, simplifiant le traitement et réduisant les coûts par rapport aux méthodes actuelles. Les patients atteints d’angio-œdème héréditaire pourraient éviter des médicaments à vie et des procédures compliquées. Cette approche pourrait aussi faciliter les thérapies géniques pour d’autres maladies.

**Prochaine étape** – La FDA examinera les données de sécurité et d’efficacité avant de décider. En parallèle, les chercheurs continueront à suivre les patients et à améliorer l’édition génique in vivo pour réduire les risques comme les modifications génétiques non désirées ou les réactions immunitaires.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Une nouvelle thérapie génique qui modifie les gènes directement dans le corps montre un succès durable et pourrait bientôt devenir le premier traitement CRISPR in vivo approuvé par la FDA pour l’angio-œdème héréditaire.
articles.personality_title_es: Primera terapia génica CRISPR dentro del cuerpo cerca de aprobación FDA tras 4 años de éxito
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El angioedema hereditario es una enfermedad genética rara que causa hinchazón dolorosa en la garganta y otras partes del cuerpo. Las terapias génicas actuales con CRISPR requieren sacar y editar las células fuera del cuerpo antes de devolverlas, lo que hace el tratamiento complicado y costoso.

**Qué pasó** – Intellia Therapeutics desarrolló un nuevo tratamiento llamado lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z) que edita genes directamente dentro del cuerpo. Esta terapia usa pequeñas partículas grasas para llevar el sistema CRISPR al hígado y apagar un gen que causa hinchazón. Los datos muestran que el tratamiento sigue siendo efectivo cuatro años después de una sola infusión. Intellia solicitó la aprobación de la Administración de Alimentos y Medicamentos de Estados Unidos (FDA), con una decisión esperada para el 10 de marzo de 2027.

**Impacto** – Si se aprueba, lonvo-z será la primera terapia CRISPR entregada dentro del cuerpo, simplificando el tratamiento y reduciendo costos comparado con los métodos actuales. Los pacientes con angioedema hereditario podrían evitar medicamentos de por vida y procedimientos complicados. Este método podría abrir la puerta a terapias génicas más fáciles para otras enfermedades.

**Próximo paso** – La FDA revisará los datos de seguridad y eficacia antes de decidir sobre la aprobación. Mientras tanto, los investigadores continuarán monitoreando a los pacientes y mejorando la edición genética dentro del cuerpo para minimizar riesgos como cambios genéticos no deseados o reacciones inmunes.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Una nueva terapia génica que edita genes directamente dentro del cuerpo muestra éxito duradero y podría convertirse pronto en el primer tratamiento CRISPR in vivo aprobado por la FDA para el angioedema hereditario.
